Q: Changing time zone A:

To approach this, I would first make it clear what the data is that you are viewing and then go about trying to modify it into a view that makes sense for your use case. I would clearly label or understand the time zone that you are starting with and then convert it to the time zone the students are located.

This will get a bit more complicated if the students are not all located in the same time zone. To try and make easier to understand I would convert the recorded time to UTC and then have an additional column for what time zone the students are located. We can then use this to vary the formula on how we get the output columns.

I have assumed a -5 for the UTC conversion example

There are a few things to watch out for when working with time zones first one being daylight savings. Regions go into it at different times and it can make this more complicated.

Q: Why can't I use Iterable as a type for overloading a singledispatchmethod? A:

Root Cause: typing.Iterable is not a type

The error comes from singledispatch's internal _is_valid_dispatch_type() check, which requires the registered class to be an actual type instance:

def _is_valid_dispatch_type(cls):
    if isinstance(cls, type):
        return True
    ...
    return False

typing.Iterable is a _SpecialGenericAlias — a typing construct, not a class:

>>> import typing, numbers
>>> type(typing.Iterable)
<class 'typing._SpecialGenericAlias'>
>>> isinstance(typing.Iterable, type)
False

>>> type(numbers.Number)
<class 'abc.ABCMeta'>
>>> isinstance(numbers.Number, type)
True   # ABCMeta is a metaclass — Number is a real class

numbers.Number is a genuine ABC class whose metaclass is ABCMeta. typing.Iterable is a wrapper that supports isinstance() checks at runtime by delegating to collections.abc.Iterable, but it is not itself a type.

Fix: use collections.abc.Iterable

from functools import singledispatch
from collections.abc import Iterable  # ← not typing.Iterable
from numbers import Number

@singledispatch
def handle(x):
    print("Fallback")

@handle.register(Iterable)
def _(x):
    print("I'm an iterable")

@handle.register(Number)
def _(x):
    print("I'm a number")

collections.abc.Iterable is the underlying ABC that typing.Iterable wraps. It has ABCMeta as its metaclass, so isinstance(collections.abc.Iterable, type) is True and registration succeeds.

How numbers.Number works without being in int.__mro__

This is the part that "fascinates" you. singledispatch doesn't just walk the literal MRO — it uses _compose_mro() to build an extended MRO that includes registered ABCs for which issubclass(cls, abc) is true. Since numbers.ABCMeta defines __subclasshook__ to make issubclass(int, numbers.Number) return True, numbers.Number gets spliced into the composed MRO at dispatch time.

The same mechanism works for collections.abc.Iterable.

Caveats with Iterable dispatch

Two things to watch out for:

1. Strings are iterable — handle("foo") will dispatch to your Iterable handler unless you register str explicitly with a higher priority:

@handle.register(str)
def _(x):
    print("I'm a string")

2. Dispatch ambiguity — if a type is a virtual subclass of both registered ABCs (e.g., a numeric type that's also iterable), singledispatch raises a RuntimeError about ambiguous dispatch. Register the more specific type explicitly to resolve it.

Q: How can we add Google Pay or Apple pay in stripe hosted checkout page? A:

Material Used : WordPress Site, WooCommerce Plugin with stripe add-on & connected with stipe account, Elementor as a page builder.

Query : I was unable to see google pay & apple pay on my website in cart page, checkout page and single product page.

Things to know : Apple pay will only visible on iOS devices, if you are checking on android it won't because android don't use apple pay as wallet. | Google pay can be visible on both platform iOS & Android but a device must be a handset won't visible on desktop . | In stripe account you must be verified that you are using which country and which currency is accepted by the country in that case try using VPN to get assured for the currency conflict.

Solution : At my first half I had tried every possible way to figure out the issue, the issue was the Woo-Commerce integration with the Elementor, as a woocommerce widgit block was previously used to make the desired layout of the checkout page but this was the issue, when i disabled the page & transformed it with Gutenberg editor by pasting the checkout page short code of woocommerce, this solved my issue of not being showing of google pay and apple pay on the checkout page.

Q: My code is very long. Is there a way to shorten it? A:

It's safe to say that my answer isn't what you asked for.
You want shorter code, and I'm giving you longer code.
I am a big fan of not repeating code (writing less, reusing, simplicity), but I also think about extensions. In this case, I opt for the latter, like the excellent answer from J_H, I prefer longer code so that extending it is extremely simple.
I'm not going to elaborate on the ambivalent use of zone, as J_H's excellent answer already does so, so let's move on to the code:

import random as rand

  # although the operation is the same (as long as you do not
  # need to reuse its original value), we assign new names to
  # avoid confusion.
zoneIndex = rand.randint( 1, 20 )
subzoneIndex = rand.randint( 1, 10 )

zone = ""
subzone = ""

  # list of "zones"
zones = [ "water", "forest", "plain", "stone" ]

  # list of "subzones" for each "zone"
subzones = [
    [],
    [],
    [ "", "with deef", "with cows", "with horses" ],
    [ "marbel", "iron", "" ]
]

  # "zone" limits
zoneLimits = [ 5, 11, 18 ]

  # idem
subzoneLimits = [ 
    [],
    [],
    [ 2, 5, 8 ],
    [ 4, 7 ]
]

  # he only difference with “getZone()” is that the indices and
  # corresponding values are in a two-dimensional array.
def getSubzone( zoneIndex, subzoneIndex ):
    global subzone
    if zoneIndex < 2: 
        subzone = ""
        return
    for k in range( len( subzoneLimits[ zoneIndex ] ) ):
        if subzoneIndex < subzoneLimits[ zoneIndex ][ k ]:
            subzone = subzones[ zoneIndex ][ k ]
            break
        
    if subzone == "":
        subzone = subzones[ zoneIndex ][ k + 1 ]
    

def getZone( zoneIndex, subzoneIndex ):
    global zone
    
      # since the length of **zoneLimits ** is less than that of **zones**,
      # we iterate until the last position of **zoneLimits **, and if we
      # have not assigned any value to **zone**, we assign it the value
      # of the last item of **zones**.
    for i in range( len( zoneLimits )):
        if zoneIndex < zoneLimits[ i ]:
            zone = zones[ i ]
            break
        
    if zone == "":
        zone = zones[ i + 1 ]

      # call to "getSubzone()", passing as parameters the index of the
      # zone that has just been determined and the index of the subzone
    getSubzone( zones.index( zone ), subzoneIndex  )

getZone( zoneIndex, subzoneIndex )
print( f"{zone} {subzone}" )

Q: Format strings c++ A:

Here are a couple of alternatives:

  1. Use std::to_string and string concatenation:

     std::string filename = "table" + std::to_string(i) + ".dat";

  2. Use std::ostringstream:

     std::ostringstream iss;
 iss << "table" << i << ".dat";
 std::string filename = iss.str();

Using std::ostringstream also allows for things like formatting, as in using four digits with leading zeros for the number.

Newer versions of the C++ standard includes the main parts of the fmt formatting library, like std::format, which makes it even simpler:

auto filename = std::format("table{}.dat", i)

You can also use std::filesystem::path to work exclusively with paths and filenames.
